KUBERNETES POD SECURITY CHECK · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER

What are your Kubernetes manifests handing to the node?

One privileged: true, a hostPath to docker.sock, hostNetwork: true or a container running as root can turn a bug in one pod into control of the node. Paste your own Pod, Deployment, StatefulSet, DaemonSet, Job or CronJob YAML below and this page lists each risky setting with its line, the resource and container, the risk, and the exact YAML fix.

Nothing is uploaded. The YAML you paste is read in this browser and never leaves your device, and this tool makes no network calls of its own. It is a heuristic line scan, not a YAML parser, not a security audit and not a compliance claim.

1. Paste your manifest

Paste the contents of your own manifest. Multi-document files separated by --- work. Add more blocks for more files, and give each its real file name so findings point at the right file. Render Helm charts first with helm template.

Paste at least one manifest above and click Check.

Findings

File : LineResourceTypeRiskFix

Heuristic line scan, not a YAML parser, not a security audit and not a compliance claim. Review each finding yourself.

Prefer a CLI, or want this in your own CI?

Same logic, zero dependencies, one file:

python3 check.py                        # scan *.yaml / *.yml under the current directory
python3 check.py deploy.yaml k8s/       # scan specific files or directories
python3 check.py --format json          # machine-readable
python3 check.py --fail-on-risk         # exit 2 on any medium or high finding

Get check.py from the repo — stdlib only, nothing to install, no network calls. It skips node_modules, vendor, .git, build folders and Helm template files.

Common questions

What makes a Kubernetes pod spec risky?

Settings that hand a container the node or leak a credential: privileged: true, hostNetwork, hostPID or hostIPC, hostPath volumes such as /etc or the Docker socket, capabilities like SYS_ADMIN or ALL, a missing allowPrivilegeEscalation: false, running as root, a writable root filesystem, :latest images and passwords written as literal env values. Any one of them can turn a bug in one container into control of the node.

Why is privileged: true dangerous in Kubernetes?

A privileged container gets nearly every Linux capability and access to the node's devices, so a compromised process can mount the node filesystem, load kernel modules and escape to the host. Almost every real need is narrower: add one capability such as NET_ADMIN under capabilities.add, and keep privileged off.

What should securityContext contain?

A sensible baseline per container is allowPrivilegeEscalation: false, runAsNonRoot: true with a numeric runAsUser, readOnlyRootFilesystem: true, capabilities drop: [ALL] and seccompProfile type RuntimeDefault. Add back only what the workload demonstrably needs.

Does this tool send my manifests anywhere?

No. It makes no network calls at all. The YAML you paste is scanned in this page and never leaves your device, and secret values are never printed in the results.

Does a clean scan mean my cluster is secure?

No. This is a heuristic line scan, not a YAML parser, a full audit or a compliance claim. It reads only the patterns listed here, does not expand Helm templates, Kustomize overlays or anchors, and cannot see your cluster's admission policies, RBAC, network policies or images. Have a qualified person review anything that protects valuable data.

More: which Kubernetes pod settings are risky, and how do you fix each one?

what-is-kubernetes-pod-security.html.text:
← Kubernetes Pod Security Check

Kubernetes pod security: privileged, hostPath, root and how to fix each

A pod spec decides how much of the node each container can touch. Most pod-related incidents are not clever exploits. They are one setting that removed a boundary, such as a privileged container, a mounted Docker socket or a password committed in plain text.

# hands the node to the container
spec:
  hostNetwork: true
  containers:
    - name: app
      image: web:latest
      securityContext:
        privileged: true

# baseline per container
      securityContext:
        allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
        runAsNonRoot: true
        runAsUser: 10001
        readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
        capabilities:
          drop: [ALL]
        seccompProfile:
          type: RuntimeDefault

The fifteen patterns a line scan can find

  • k8s-privileged — privileged: true. Fix: set it false or delete it; add one capability instead. High.
  • k8s-host-namespace — hostNetwork, hostPID or hostIPC true. Fix: delete it. High.
  • k8s-hostpath-sensitive — hostPath of /, /etc, /root, /proc, /sys, /var/lib/kubelet or the Docker socket. Fix: emptyDir, ConfigMap, Secret or a PersistentVolumeClaim. High.
  • k8s-dangerous-capability — capabilities.add of ALL, SYS_ADMIN, NET_ADMIN, SYS_PTRACE, SYS_MODULE or DAC_READ_SEARCH. Fix: drop: [ALL] and add back one narrow capability. High.
  • k8s-literal-secret-env — a PASSWORD, SECRET, TOKEN or API_KEY set to a literal value: in env. Fix: a Secret and secretKeyRef, then rotate. The tool never prints the value. High.
  • k8s-privilege-escalation — allowPrivilegeEscalation true or unset (Kubernetes defaults it to true). Fix: set it false. Medium.
  • k8s-runs-as-root — runAsUser: 0, runAsNonRoot: false, or neither runAsNonRoot: true nor a non-zero runAsUser. Fix: runAsNonRoot: true and runAsUser: 10001. Medium.
  • k8s-hostpath-volume — any other hostPath volume. Fix: emptyDir or a PersistentVolumeClaim, or mount it read-only. Medium.
  • k8s-image-latest — an image with no tag or :latest. Fix: pin a version or digest. Medium.
  • k8s-host-port — hostPort used. Fix: expose the pod through a Service. Medium.
  • k8s-no-security-context — a container with no securityContext at all. Fix: add the baseline block shown below. Medium.
  • k8s-capabilities-not-dropped — capabilities.drop does not include ALL. Fix: drop: [ALL]. Low.
  • k8s-writable-root-fs — readOnlyRootFilesystem not true. Fix: set it true and mount an emptyDir where the app writes. Low.
  • k8s-automount-token — automountServiceAccountToken not false on the pod. Fix: set it false unless the workload calls the Kubernetes API. Low.
  • k8s-seccomp-missing — no seccompProfile on the container or pod, or type Unconfined. Fix: type: RuntimeDefault. Low.

What is a good baseline securityContext for a Kubernetes container?

Set allowPrivilegeEscalation: false, runAsNonRoot: true with a numeric runAsUser, readOnlyRootFilesystem: true, capabilities drop: [ALL] and seccompProfile type RuntimeDefault. Mount an emptyDir for any path the app must write, and add back only the capability the workload demonstrably needs.

Is a hostPath volume to /var/run/docker.sock safe?

No. The Docker API is root on the node: a pod that can reach it can start another container with the node filesystem mounted. Mounting it read-only does not restrict the API. Use a build tool that does not need the daemon, or a socket proxy that exposes only the required endpoints.

Does the default Kubernetes setup run containers as root?

Often yes. If neither the pod nor the container sets runAsNonRoot or runAsUser, the container runs as whatever user the image declares, which is frequently root. allowPrivilegeEscalation also defaults to true. Setting both explicitly removes the guesswork.

Check your own manifests

Paste your YAML into Kubernetes Pod Security Check to see every finding with its line, resource, container, risk and fix, or run the CLI in your own repository:

python3 check.py --fail-on-risk

That exits with a nonzero status on any medium or high finding, so you can wire it into your own CI. Expect some findings to be deliberate (a node agent may truly need hostPath or a capability); review each one.
